correctness.rationale: For a product of fields, vertices are precisely nonempty proper support subsets and adjacency is nonempty support intersection. A two-vertex set is total dominating exactly when the supports intersect and cover all coordinates. This criterion both constructs the minima for r>=3 and rules them out for r=2; a two-vertex total set is automatically paired. The enumerator follows from a three-class surjection count.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The strongest same-object domination theorems determine only ordinary domination. Ordinary domination does not imply total or paired domination because selected vertices need not dominate one another.

evidence: The known ordinary value \(\gamma=2\) is compatible with a dominating pair whose two vertices are nonadjacent; thus it cannot imply total or paired domination.
The 2014 article explicitly observes that the two-field product has exactly two nonadjacent ideal vertices, which yields the strengthened-domination obstruction.
Neither inspected ordinary-domination theorem classifies all dominating pairs or counts the adjacent covering pairs.

originality.rationale: The inspected primary literature establishes ordinary domination number two for products of fields and structural facts about the same ideal-intersection graphs, but it does not state total domination, paired domination, the two-factor obstruction, the minimum-set classification, or the closed enumerator.
residual_risks: An unindexed combinatorics source on intersection graphs of subsets could contain an equivalent adjacent-covering-pair enumeration.

The numerical total-domination value for products with at least three field factors is also obtainable from broader module-intersection methods; the new content assessed here is the paired-domination boundary and the complete minimum-set classification/count.
No claim is made for products containing nonfield local factors.

value.rationale: The result gives a complete strengthened-domination classification for a canonical Artinian family already singled out by the ordinary-domination literature. It identifies the exact two-factor failure, proves total and paired minima coincide from three factors onward, characterizes every minimum pair by support intersection/covering, and gives a closed exact count.
